summary: After praying alone, Jesus asks who he is; Peter answers “the Christ of God”, and Jesus speaks of the suffering that must come.

context.title: The Christ of God
paragraphs: Luke sets this scene straight after the feeding of the five thousand, passing over everything Mark recounts between that miracle and Peter’s confession. [c1] He gives no place name, and Caesarea Philippi, named by Matthew and Mark, does not appear. [c2] Only Luke says that Jesus was praying, a detail he stresses at other turning points such as the baptism. [c3]

The crowd’s answers, John the Baptist, Elijah or one of the ancient prophets, repeat the rumours that had reached Herod the tetrarch in 9:7-8. [c4] The Pulpit Commentary links them to a popular hope that great figures of Israel’s past would reappear before the Messiah. [c5] The Cambridge Bible sees Peter’s reply as the first open confession of Jesus as the Christ. [c6]

Jesus then orders silence and, for the first time, speaks explicitly of his coming death. [c7] The elders, chief priests and scribes he names were the three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the council of the nation, so the prediction concerns the nation’s leadership. [c8]

translationNotes.summary: Only Luke has “the Christ of God”; christos means “anointed”, the Greek rendering of Messiah.
translationNotes.body: Christos means anointed and stands in the Septuagint for the Hebrew mashiach, Messiah. [c9] Each Gospel words Peter’s answer differently, and this exact form is Luke’s own. [c10] It echoes Luke 2:26, where Simeon is promised that he will see the Lord’s Christ. [c11] A. B. Bruce thinks the wording reflects the language of the apostolic age, while Mark’s shorter form sounds more original. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Epitimao often means “rebuke”, but here it is a stern charge to keep silent, not a reproof of Peter’s answer.
translationNotes.body: Epitimao commonly means to rebuke or censure, but Thayer files this verse under a milder sense, to admonish or charge sharply. [c13] Vincent traces the word to laying a penalty on someone, hence a solemn charge under penalty. [c14] Meyer reads the order as restraining the disciples’ ardour, so that their confession would not run ahead of the suffering that God’s plan still required. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: Dei, “it is necessary”, frames the suffering of the Son of Man as part of God’s purpose.
translationNotes.body: Dei is an impersonal verb meaning it is necessary, and Thayer lists a sense of necessity established by the counsel and decree of God. [c16] Meyer reads it that way here and points to Luke 24:26. [c17] There the risen Jesus uses the same verb when he asks whether the Christ did not have to suffer these things. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Apodokimazo means to reject after scrutiny, the verb used for the builders’ rejected stone in Psalm 118.
translationNotes.body: Apodokimazo means to disapprove or reject, and Vincent stresses rejection on scrutiny or trial, a deliberate verdict. [c19] Luke uses the same verb in 20:17, where Jesus cites Psalm 118:22 about the stone the builders rejected. [c20] John Gill reads the prediction as fulfilling Psalm 118:22, where the stone the builders rejected becomes the head of the corner. [c21]

claims.text: Luke moves directly from the feeding of the five thousand to Peter’s confession, passing over the material of Mark 6:45-8:26.
Luke does not mention Caesarea Philippi, which Matthew and Mark name as the setting of Peter’s confession.
Only Luke records that Jesus was praying before asking the question, and Luke stresses Jesus’ prayer at other moments such as his baptism (Lk 3:21).
The answers in Luke 9:19 (John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the ancient prophets) match the reports that perplexed Herod the tetrarch in Luke 9:7-8.
The Pulpit Commentary relates the crowd’s answers to a popular expectation that certain great national figures would reappear before the Messiah.
The Cambridge Bible regards Peter’s answer as the first time that Jesus’ identity as the Christ was openly recognised and confessed.
Luke 9:22 is Jesus’ first explicit announcement of his approaching death.
The elders, chief priests and scribes named in Luke 9:22 were the three sections that formed the Sanhedrin, the great council of the nation.
Χριστός means anointed, and in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach).
Each evangelist gives Peter’s confession differently, and the form “the Christ of God” is peculiar to Luke.
Luke 2:26 says Simeon would not die before seeing τὸν χριστὸν κυρίου, the Lord’s Christ, an expression akin to “the Christ of God”.
A. B. Bruce, in the Expositor’s Greek Testament, holds that Luke’s form of the confession reflects the language of the apostolic age and that Mark’s form is original by comparison.
Thayer gives ἐπιτιμάω the senses rebuke or censure, but lists Luke 9:21 under a milder sense, to admonish or charge sharply.
Vincent explains ἐπιτιμήσας as an emphatic, solemn charge, from the sense of laying a penalty on someone.
Meyer understands the command to silence as quenching the ardour of the confession so that it would not interfere with the divine appointment of the Messiah’s sufferings.
Δεῖ is an impersonal verb meaning it is necessary, and Thayer lists a sense of necessity established by the counsel and decree of God, used especially of Christ’s sufferings.
Meyer reads the δεῖ of Luke 9:22 as the appointment of God, citing Luke 24:26.
In Luke 24:26 the risen Jesus uses the same verb (ἔδει) in asking whether the Christ had to suffer.
Ἀποδοκιμάζω means to disapprove or reject, and Vincent explains it as rejection on scrutiny or trial, implying deliberate rejection.
Luke 20:17 uses the same verb (ἀπεδοκίμασαν) in quoting Psalm 118:22 about the stone the builders rejected.
John Gill reads the rejection foretold in Luke 9:22 as fulfilling Psalm 118:22, where the stone the builders rejected becomes the head of the corner.
